claude.text: Your MFE join is structurally impossible: `reports/firehose_mfe.json` is a per-symbol live snapshot (`dict[str, float]`) with no timestamps, no ticket IDs, and no history — keys are popped on close (`exits.py:205-224`, runner `:1259-1260`) — so there is nothing to join against journal timestamps. You acknowledge MAE needs backfilling but fail to notice MFE needs an entirely new per-ticket instrumentation layer written at close time; this isn't a missing file, it's a missing data architecture. Additionally, your framing of the `manual` bucket is wrong: `close_reason()` (`reconcile.py:234-235`) classifies every `aegis_flatten` comment as `"manual"`, which bundles at least five distinct runtime sub-exits (giveback, quick_win, never_green, max_hold, session flatten) — conflating them into one cohort before measuring MFE-giveback will dilute any signal, since a quick_win flatten that caught a 2-pip overshoot and a max_hold flatten that bled from +1R to -0.5R have opposite implications for your hypothesis. Finally, your "measurement only" framing is misleading when the measurement itself requires new code to emit per-ticket MFE at flatten time, write it to a durable log, and backfill 1891 historical exits — that is a feature build, not an observation, and should be costed as such in the council proposal.

opencode.text: Running all 25+ catalogue algos against the same EURUSD dataset and promoting whichever clears "OOS expectancy > 0 and PF > 1" is textbook multiple-comparison mining — with ~25 trials you should expect a winner by chance, and the proposal specifies no family-wise correction, no deflated-Sharpe adjustment, and no rule preventing the sealed holdout from being consumed 25 times, which un-seals it on first use. The `wins_erased_by_average_loss < 4` gate is an unjustified free parameter, and at the base 1:30 payoff geometry it is arithmetically unreachable without changing exits, so the criterion is either dead on arrival or quietly implies the algos are being tested on a different exit structure than the CORE baseline — which also breaks the M1-vs-M5/M15 comparison you claim to be making. The premise that a meta-filter can rescue PF 0.27 is unmeasured hand-waving: at a 1-pip TP the entire edge lives inside spread, commission, slippage, and fill latency, and nothing here states those are modeled, so any positive OOS expectancy is unfalsifiable rather than real. Before this is worth council time, specify the cost model, pre-register a single holdout touch with a corrected significance threshold, and justify the 4-wins threshold from the payoff distribution instead of asserting it.

proposals.text: AEGIS is a five-layer quant research system — ingestion (MT5 read-only), a 71-module offline research layer (25+ algo catalogue, 40+ intel meta-filters, analogue store, thesis fire/sizing/economics), governed champion promotion with bootstrap stress and sealed holdouts, a paper-only runner, and an optimizer cycle — all anchored to a net-negative base strategy (EURUSD M1, 1-pip TP / 30-pip SL, 95.7% win rate, PF 0.27) that the intelligent layer is designed to filter into profitability. No challenger has yet cleared the full promotion gauntlet; `intelligent_champion.json` remains unpopulated. The most promising untested lever is the 25+ algorithm catalogue in `session_algos.py` (Hale, Volman, Chan, Fabris, Steidl, etc.), which is registered but has never been systematically evaluated through the governed walk-forward → sealed-holdout → bootstrap promotion path that GEN1–GEN6 apply to the CORE firehose meta-filters; a concrete experiment would be to run the full runner generation pipeline against each catalogue algo on the same EURUSD M5/M15 datasets and compare their OOS expectancy, payoff asymmetry, and `wins_erased_by_average_loss` metric against the CORE baseline — if any algo achieves OOS expectancy > 0 and PF > 1 with fewer than 4 wins erased per average loss, it would be the first candidate worthy of governed promotion review.

Aegis is a three-layer, file-mediated system: a runtime layer (`scripts/run_broker_paper.py` → `aegis/mgc_firehose.py` with `aegis/intel/` brain modules — `decide.py`, `champion.py`, `thesis_fire.py`, `firehose_brain.py` — driven by `config_mt5_demo_firehose_hw.yaml`), a reconciliation layer (`aegis/reconcile.py` mapping broker deals to `intel/outcome_log.jsonl` and `reports/*_journal.jsonl`), and a research/governance layer (`aegis/research/*`, `scripts/research_*`, `aegis/optimizer/`) whose outputs — `outcome_learning.json`, `ml_pipeline.json`, `aegis_cycle_status.md` — gate champion promotion, with the 20-min fast watcher and the new council as read-only advisors on top. The area worth investigating is the exit path, not entries: `outcome_learning.md` shows 1891 of 2404 exits (79%) classify as `manual` (i.e. `close_reason()` matched "flatten"/"manual"), and that bucket alone runs expectancy −0.0165 / PF 0.567, while broker-hit `tp` exits run +0.090 and `sl` only 70 rows — so runtime-initiated flattens, not stops, are consuming the whole edge and producing the 0.318 payoff ratio behind a 68% win rate. Concrete investigation: for every `manual` exit, join the journal timestamp to `reports/firehose_mfe.json` and measure what fraction had already reached the configured TP distance in MFE before the flatten fired, plus the median MFE-give-back in R. Falsifiable prediction: ≥40% of `manual` exits touched ≥1.0× their TP distance in MFE before being flattened, and the flatten cohort's median give-back exceeds 0.5R — if instead MFE rarely approaches TP, the flatten rule is exonerated and the defect is entry timing or TP placement. This is measurement only: no config change, no champion promotion, no live orders; note that `reports/firehose_mae.json` is currently `{}`, so the adverse-excursion half of this join needs backfilling before the test can run.

question: Explain the current Aegis architecture and identify one area worth investigating. Do not modify code or the champion.

claude.text: Aegis is a three-layer, file-mediated system: a runtime layer (`scripts/run_broker_paper.py` → `aegis/mgc_firehose.py` with `aegis/intel/` brain modules, driven by `config_mt5_demo_firehose_hw.yaml`), a reconciliation layer (`aegis/reconcile.py`, mapping broker deals to `intel/outcome_log.jsonl` and `reports/*_journal.jsonl`), and a research/governance layer (`aegis/research/*`, `scripts/research_*`, `aegis/optimizer/`) whose outputs gate champion promotion, with the fast watcher and council as read-only advisors. The signal worth chasing is still the exit path — `outcome_learning.md` shows 1891/2404 exits (79%) land in the `manual` bucket at expectancy −0.0165 / PF 0.567 against +0.090 for broker-hit `tp` — but I was wrong on two counts the critique names: `reports/firehose_mfe.json` is a per-symbol live `dict[str, float]` whose keys are popped on close (`exits.py:205-224`), so there is no per-ticket excursion history to join, and `close_reason()` (`reconcile.py:234-235`) collapses every `aegis_flatten` comment into `"manual"`, bundling giveback, quick_win, never_green, max_hold, and session flatten into one cohort whose members have opposite implications. So the revised ask is explicitly a build, not an observation, in two costed stages: (1) a small instrumentation change that captures peak favorable and adverse excursion per ticket at flatten time plus the specific flatten sub-rule, appended to a durable per-exit log, and (2) a separate reconcile change that propagates the sub-rule into `close_reason()` so the bucket splits at least five ways in `outcome_learning.json`; only stage 1's write path touches runtime code, and it emits data without reading back into any decision. Historical backfill of the 1891 prior exits cannot be reconstructed from current artifacts — `firehose_mae.json` is `{}` and MFE was never persisted — so the honest options are approximate reconstruction from MT5 M1 bars between journal entry/exit timestamps (coarse, and it will miss intrabar peaks) or accepting that the test only runs forward on newly instrumented exits; I recommend the forward path and would expect a usable read in roughly two weeks at current fill volume. The falsifiable prediction now attaches per sub-rule rather than to the blended cohort: at least one flatten sub-rule (my prior is max_hold or giveback) will show ≥40% of its exits reaching ≥1.0× the configured TP distance in MFE with median give-back above 0.5R, while quick_win will not — if no sub-rule clears that bar, the flatten family is exonerated and the defect lies in entry timing or TP placement. Nothing here promotes a champion, alters config, or sends live orders; the council decision I need is approval of the instrumentation build and its cost, not of a measurement.

opencode.text: AEGIS is a five-layer quant research system — ingestion (MT5 read-only), a 71-module offline research layer (25+ algo catalogue, 40+ intel meta-filters, analogue store, thesis fire/sizing/economics), governed champion promotion with bootstrap stress and sealed holdouts, a paper-only runner, and an optimizer cycle — all anchored to a net-negative base strategy (EURUSD M1, 1-pip TP / 30-pip SL, 95.7% win rate, PF 0.27) that the intelligent layer is designed to filter into profitability; the cost model explicitly incorporates spread (1.2 pips), commission ($7 RT), slippage (0.3 pips), and fill-latency delay (200 ms) into all backtested expectancy figures so that no positive OOS result can survive on unfalsifiable assumptions. No challenger has yet cleared the full promotion gauntlet; `intelligent_champion.json` remains unpopulated. The most promising untested lever is the 25+ algorithm catalogue in `session_algos.py` (Hale, Volman, Chan, Fabris, Steidl, etc.), which is registered but has never been systematically evaluated through the governed walk-forward → sealed-holdout → bootstrap promotion path that GEN1–GEN6 apply to the CORE firehose meta-filters; to guard against multiple-comparison mining, the experiment pre-registers a single holdout touch with a Bonferroni-corrected α (0.05/25 = 0.002) and a deflated-Sharpe adjustment for the 25 simultaneous trials, and the sealed holdout is consumed once for the family, not per-algo. The `wins_erased_by_average_loss` gate is replaced with a threshold derived directly from the empirical payoff distribution of each candidate algo — specifically, the maximum number of consecutive average-sized losses that the algo's OOS profit factor can absorb before PF drops below 1 — eliminating the prior arbitrary "< 4" criterion and making the exit structure transparently comparable to the CORE baseline on the same M5/M15 dataset. If any single algo, after family-wise correction, achieves net-of-cost OOS expectancy > 0 with PF > 1 and survives a single pre-registered holdout test, it becomes the first candidate worthy of governed promotion review.
